raspberry.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

8.type_note_seasoned: Raspberry is marginal in the St. George Dixie: the hot, low, alkaline core is the ground Utah State University Extension flags as difficult, and the county's dependable raspberry ground is its higher-elevation towns instead. The best bet here is a heat-tolerant, low-chill, fall-bearing (primocane) type, because its fall crop ripens after the peak summer heat and avoids fruit sunburn (USU Extension); good choices are Caroline, Josephine, Polana, Joan J, and Polka, or the low-chill desert canes Bababerry and Dorman Red. Give it afternoon shade, mulch heavily, correct the alkaline-soil iron chlorosis with a chelated iron, and water steadily.
8.type_note_beginner: Raspberry is a tough crop for the hot, low St. George Dixie. Choose a heat-tolerant, low-chill, fall-bearing type such as Caroline, Josephine, or Polana, whose berries ripen in fall after the worst heat. Give it afternoon shade and deep mulch, treat yellowing leaves with a chelated iron, and water it steadily. It will not be an easy or long-lived planting here.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is not the main risk for raspberry here; the summer heat and the alkaline soil are. Because the fall crop ripens into October, an early freeze near the November 1 first frost can cut the tail of the harvest short, so pick steadily through the fall.
8.grown_as_note_seasoned: In the St. George Dixie a raspberry is grown as a deciduous, fall-bearing cane fruit, planted dormant in late winter and cut back hard in the dormant season so it fruits on the new primocanes. It flowers in mid-summer and ripens its crop in the cooler fall, after the peak heat, then rests through winter. Only low-chill, heat-tolerant types persist in this hot, alkaline ground, and even those are best treated as a short-lived planting rather than a dependable one.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: In the St. George Dixie, raspberries are grown as a fall-bearing type, planted dormant in late winter and cut to the ground each winter so the new canes carry the crop. They flower in summer and ripen berries in fall, after the worst heat. Only special low-chill types keep going in this hot, alkaline soil, and even those may not last many years.

raspberry.region_notes_beginner: Raspberry is a hard crop in the hot, low St. George Dixie, and it grows best up in the county's higher-elevation towns. If you want to try it here, choose a heat-tolerant, low-chill, fall-bearing (primocane) type such as Caroline, Josephine, Polana, Joan J, or Polka, whose berries ripen in fall after the worst heat has passed. Plant dormant canes in late winter, give them afternoon shade and deep mulch, and water steadily. The alkaline desert soil often yellows the leaves, which a chelated iron treatment fixes. Expect a small, hard-won crop.
raspberry.region_notes_seasoned: Raspberry is marginal in the St. George Dixie core: this is a hot, low, alkaline-soil site, the kind Utah State University Extension flags as difficult for the crop, while the county's dependable raspberry ground is its higher-elevation towns above the valley. The steer here is toward heat-tolerant, low-chill, fall-bearing (primocane) types, because in Utah's Dixie their fruit ripens after the hottest part of the summer is over and so escapes the sunburn that scorches a summer crop (USU Extension). Look to the fall-bearing cultivars Caroline, Josephine, Polana, Joan J, and Polka, or the low-chill desert canes Bababerry and Dorman Red. Plant dormant canes in late winter, and expect the alkaline soil to drive iron chlorosis, so treat yellowing leaves with a chelated iron. Give the planting afternoon shade to cut sunburn, mulch the shallow roots, use raised beds in heavy soil, and water steadily through the dry heat. Even managed well, treat this as a hard-won, shorter-lived planting than a cooler climate would give.

blackberry.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

8.type_note_seasoned: Blackberry is marginal in the St. George Dixie: USU Extension's Washington County fruit guidance places it with the crops for the county's higher-elevation towns, not the low-elevation valley, so the hot, alkaline core is a stretch. Choose low-chill, heat-tolerant erect or semi-erect types, give the planting afternoon shade, mulch heavily, and water steadily through the summer.
8.type_note_beginner: Blackberry is a stretch in the hot, low St. George Dixie and does better in the county's higher-elevation towns. Choose a low-chill, heat-tolerant erect or semi-erect type, give it afternoon shade, and water it generously.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Blackberry blooms in early spring, when the late frosts that run to the end of March can still catch open flowers, so cover a low planting on a hard-freeze night during bloom. Through the rest of the year the summer heat, not cold, is the greater stress on the crop.
8.grown_as_note_seasoned: Here a blackberry is grown as a deciduous cane fruit: the canes drop their leaves through the cool winter while the perennial crown lives on for many years, and each cane grows one year and fruits the next before dying. Plant dormant in late winter, prune in the dormant season to the cultivar's habit, and site it to survive the desert summers. Only low-chill, heat-tolerant types hold up in this hot, alkaline ground.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: Your blackberry loses its leaves and rests through the cool winter (this rest is called dormancy). The roots live for years, but each cane lives only two: it grows one year, then fruits and dies. Prune it in winter, plant low-chill heat-tolerant types, and manage the summer heat and alkaline soil for a modest crop.

blackberry.region_notes_beginner: Blackberry is a marginal crop in the hot, low St. George Dixie; it does better up in the county's higher-elevation towns. To try it here, pick a low-chill, heat-tolerant erect or semi-erect type, plant dormant canes in late winter, and give the planting afternoon shade and deep mulch. Late frosts into the end of March can nip the early blooms, and summer heat can scorch the berries, so it is not a sure thing. Water it steadily and expect a modest crop.
blackberry.region_notes_seasoned: Blackberry is marginal in the St. George Dixie core. Utah State University Extension's Washington County fruit guidance lists blackberries with the crops that do well in the county's higher-elevation towns, not on the low-elevation St. George thrive list, so in the hot, alkaline valley it is a stretch. If you grow it here, choose low-chill, heat-tolerant erect or semi-erect types, plant dormant canes in late winter, and site the planting for afternoon shade. Its early spring bloom is exposed to the late frosts that run to the end of March, and the summer heat can scorch ripening fruit, so it is squeezed from both sides. Mulch heavily, correct the alkaline-soil iron chlorosis, and water steadily; expect a modest, hard-won crop rather than a bumper one.

blueberry.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

8.type_note_seasoned: Blueberry is very marginal in the St. George Dixie: the native soil is strongly alkaline, hostile ground for a crop that needs acidic soil around pH 4.5 to 5.5, so it can only be grown in a large container of amended acidic mix with acidified water. Choose the lowest-chill southern highbush selections and plant two cultivars for pollination. Soil, not cold, is the binding limit here; treat it as an experiment, not a dependable harvest.
8.type_note_beginner: Blueberry is a very hard sell in the St. George Dixie. The soil is too alkaline, so it needs a large container of acidic potting mix and acidified water. Choose a low-chill southern highbush variety, plant two for pollination, and treat it as an experiment.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Low-chill southern highbush blueberries bloom early, and a late freeze can run to the end of March here, so the open flowers on a container plant carry some risk; move or cover the pot during a hard cold snap in bloom.
8.grown_as_note_seasoned: In the St. George Dixie, blueberry is a container-only crop, since the native soil is alkaline; grown in a large pot of acidic mix, it takes a real winter chill at this elevation and drops its leaves for a true dormant season. It breaks bud and blooms in early spring, when a late freeze can catch an open flower, then ripens fruit from May into June. Prune late in dormancy, just before bud break, and keep two cultivars for pollination.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: In the St. George Dixie, blueberries need a large container because the desert soil is too alkaline. The plant gets a real winter rest at this elevation and loses its leaves. It flowers in early spring, so cover it if a late frost threatens the blooms, then ripens berries in late spring and early summer. Plant two varieties so they pollinate.

blueberry.region_notes_beginner: Blueberry is very hard to grow in the St. George Dixie. The desert soil is far too alkaline for it, so it will not survive planted in the ground. Grow a low-chill southern highbush variety in a large container filled with acidic potting mix, keep the water acidified, shade it from the harshest sun, and plant two varieties so they pollinate each other. Treat any berries you get as a bonus.
blueberry.region_notes_seasoned: Blueberry is very marginal in the St. George Dixie, and the binding constraint is the soil, not the climate. The Mojave-edge desert ground is strongly alkaline, hostile to a plant that needs acidic soil around pH 4.5 to 5.5, so it cannot be grown in the open ground here at all. Grow only the lowest-chill southern highbush selections, and only in large containers filled with an amended acidic peat or pine-bark mix, with the irrigation water acidified and two cultivars set for pollination. Shield the pots from the harshest afternoon sun, cover them if a hard freeze threatens the early spring bloom, and treat any harvest as a genuine experiment rather than a dependable crop.

elderberry.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

8.type_note_seasoned: American elderberry is the type to grow in the St. George Dixie; there is no separate low-chill type. Moisture, not chill, is the binding constraint, so it depends on steady, generous irrigation, and the alkaline soil adds iron chlorosis to watch. Plant two different cultivars for cross-pollination.
8.type_note_beginner: American elderberry is the type to grow in the St. George Dixie. What it needs most is water, not cold, so irrigate it consistently and plant two different varieties.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is not the limiting factor for elderberry here; it blooms after the late-March frosts have passed and ripens through the summer. Keeping it watered through the long, hot summer is the real management task.
8.grown_as_note_seasoned: Elderberry is a permanent deciduous shrub here, planted once and kept for years, resting only briefly through the mild Dixie winter. It blooms in mid to late spring, after frost, and ripens its fruit through the summer. Keep it well watered through the heat, renew old canes in late winter, and plant two different cultivars for good fruit set.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: Your elderberry is a long-lived bush you plant once and keep for years. It rests through the mild winter, flowers in late spring, and ripens berries in summer. Keep it well watered in the heat, prune old stems in late winter, and plant two different varieties.

elderberry.region_notes_beginner: Elderberry is a marginal crop in the St. George Dixie, but a workable one if you keep it watered. It naturally grows in much wetter places than the desert, so give it steady, generous water and some afternoon shade in the summer heat. Plant two different varieties for a good crop, and treat yellowing leaves in the alkaline soil with a chelated iron.
elderberry.region_notes_seasoned: Elderberry is marginal in the St. George Dixie, and the reason is water, not cold or type. American elderberry, the type to grow, is a moisture-loving shrub native to far wetter ground than the Mojave-edge desert offers, so it depends entirely on steady, generous irrigation, with afternoon shade a real help through the summer heat that reaches 100°F from June into August (USU Extension). The alkaline soil adds iron chlorosis to manage. Plant dormant in late winter, keep two different cultivars for cross-pollination, and treat this as an irrigation-dependent planting rather than a drought-tough desert native.

strawberry.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

8.grown_as_note_seasoned: The St. George Dixie grows strawberries as a perennial matted row, not a pulled annual: a bed of June-bearing plants set in early spring lives for several productive years, giving one concentrated crop in late spring before the summer heat, then is renovated right after harvest and carried through the summer with mulch and afternoon shade. Set dormant bare-root crowns as soon as the soil can be worked, choose a site with morning sun and some afternoon shade in the hottest spots, and grow on well-drained beds, since strawberries are sensitive to salty soil and water. The alkaline desert soil can drive iron chlorosis, so correct yellowing leaves with a chelated iron.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: In the St. George Dixie, strawberries are a bed you plant once and keep for several years, not a crop you replace every year. Plant dormant crowns in early spring, pick berries in late spring before the hot summer, then mow and thin the bed and mulch it to get through the heat. Give them morning sun with some afternoon shade in the hottest spots, and plant them where water drains away well.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A late spring frost can run to the end of March here, into the strawberry bloom, and open blossoms and ripening fruit are damaged below 32°F. On a night a hard freeze is forecast during bloom, cover the bed with frost cloth beforehand and anchor the edges; mulch the crowns with straw over winter.

strawberry.region_notes_beginner: Strawberry does well in the low St. George Dixie, and you can grow it as a bed that comes back year after year. Plant dormant bare-root crowns in early spring, space them out, and let the runners fill in the row. June-bearing types give one big crop in late spring, before the summer heat; pinch off the flowers the first year so the plants grow strong. After harvest, mow the old leaves and thin the row, then mulch and shade the bed to carry it through the hot summer. Cover the blossoms if a late frost threatens into the end of March.
strawberry.region_notes_seasoned: Strawberry is a low-elevation thriver in the St. George Dixie: Utah State University Extension's Washington County fruit guidance lists strawberries among the crops that do well at the valley's low elevation, and here they are grown as a perennial matted row that lives for several years, not a bed pulled each summer. Set dormant bare-root crowns in early spring, as soon as the soil can be worked, spacing plants about 18 inches apart in rows 36 to 42 inches apart and letting runners fill the row. June-bearing types set their flower buds the previous fall and give one concentrated crop in late spring, before the worst heat; pinch off the first year's flowers to build strong plants. Renovate right after harvest, mowing the old foliage above the crowns and narrowing the row, then carry the bed through the summer with mulch and afternoon shade. Late frosts to the end of March are the main threat to open blossoms, so protect the bloom, and the alkaline soil can yellow leaves, which a chelated iron corrects.
